title: The Postal Inspector Who Invented Public Health
event_summary: During Bombay's catastrophic bubonic plague outbreak, a Russian-trained bacteriologist named Waldemar Haffkine set up a makeshift laboratory in a corridor of Grant Medical College and, working with a skeleton crew of untrained assistants, developed the world's first effective plague vaccine. He tested it on himself first, then organized mass inoculation campaigns across Indian communities that were otherwise being subjected to brutal forced quarantines, home demolitions, and invasive body searches by British plague committees. By January 1898, he had vaccinated over 8,000 people, demonstrating a mortality reduction of nearly 50-70% among the inoculated.
why_forgotten: Haffkine was later scapegoated when a contaminated batch of vaccine caused tetanus deaths in 1902 in Mulkowal, Punjab — an error traced to a careless assistant — but the British establishment used it to destroy his career and discredit Indian-produced biologics. His Jewish-Ukrainian origins and outspoken criticism of colonial health abuses made him an inconvenient figure for both British imperial narratives and later Indian nationalist historiography, which preferred homegrown heroes. The episode was buried under broader colonial shame.
why_it_matters: Haffkine's Bombay campaign established the foundational model for mass vaccination drives in the Global South, and the laboratory he built eventually became the Haffkine Institute, which still produces vaccines today and was critical to India's COVID-19 response. His work proved that large-scale preventive inoculation — rather than quarantine and punishment — was the most effective response to epidemic disease, a principle that underpins modern WHO pandemic strategy. The ethical framework he championed, of self-experimentation before public deployment, became a cornerstone of vaccine trial ethics.
